planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in well-drained garden soil in full sun, where summer rain events will trigger repeated flushes of bloom into fall.

directions: Ruth Page is one of the late Texas bulbman Thad Howard's foundational Zephyranthes hybrids, a cross of Z. rosea and Z. citrina that produces large, bright pink, upfacing flowers over flat, grassy green foliage from early summer until frost. Because it proved fertile, Howard used Ruth Page as a parent for many later named hybrids, making it a key reference point in rain lily breeding history. Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in full sun and well-drained soil, and expect a synchronized bloom flush within a few days of any good summer soaking. Leave established clumps undisturbed for several seasons to build a dense flowering colony before dividing.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery, Zephyranthes 'Ruth Page' plant description
Pacific Bulb Society, Zephyranthes Hybrids wiki page

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in well-drained garden soil in full sun; clumps bulk up over a few seasons into dense, free-flowering stands.

directions: Libra is a Thad Howard hybrid rain lily from a cross of Zephyranthes lindleyana and Zephyranthes 'Ruth Page', grown for dark pink, cup-shaped flowers carried on stalks noticeably taller than many rain lily selections. Blooms begin in early summer and repeat in flushes after warm-season rain through the growing season. Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in full sun with sharp drainage, since standing winter moisture is more likely to rot the bulbs than summer downpours. Established clumps are long-lived and need division only when crowding visibly reduces flowering.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery, Zephyranthes 'Libra' plant description
Pacific Bulb Society, Zephyranthes Hybrids wiki page

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in well-drained garden soil in full sun; bloom begins in late summer and repeats after rain into fall.

directions: Apricot Queen is a Thad Howard hybrid from a cross of Zephyranthes 'Ruth Page' and Zephyranthes pulchella, prized for color-shifting flowers that open peachy apricot on the first day and deepen to a peach-sherbet orange on the second. Glossy green foliage stays low and grassy, letting the flower spikes stand out starting in late summer and continuing with each rain until frost. Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in full sun and well-drained soil, and avoid heavy winter moisture that can rot dormant bulbs. Clumps multiply steadily and are best left undisturbed for several years before dividing.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery, Zephyranthes 'Apricot Queen' plant description
Pacific Bulb Society, Zephyranthes Hybrids wiki page

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; fast-multiplying clumps fill in within a couple of seasons.

directions: Zephyranthes reginae takes its common name from Valles, San Luis Potosi in eastern Mexico, where plantsman Thad Howard first collected it in the 1950s. Narrow, tufted green foliage is topped from midsummer until frost with dozens of bright lemon-yellow, silver-dollar-sized flowers that appear in a synchronized flush two to three days after rain. Unlike many rain lilies that demand full sun and lean, dry conditions, this species performs best with regular moisture and tolerates light shade, making it a good match for the edge of a border or woodland path. Divide congested clumps in early spring once flowering starts to taper off from overcrowding.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery, Zephyranthes reginae plant description
Pacific Bulb Society, Zephyranthes species wiki page

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in well-drained garden soil in full sun; container culture is a safe option where winters run colder than zone 8.

directions: Zephyranthes mesochloa is a South American species native from Brazil through Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern Argentina, bearing white to soft pink funnel-shaped flowers on slender stems above grassy, glossy foliage. Like its Gulf Coast relatives, it stays dormant through dry spells and blooms in a quick, synchronized flush within days of a soaking summer rain. Because its cold tolerance is less documented than well-known Gulf Coast species such as Z. candida or Z. drummondii, treat it as a zone 8-10 plant and consider heavy mulch or container culture at the colder end of its range. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage, and divide congested clumps in spring as flowering begins to decline.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online, Zephyranthes mesochloa taxon page
Pacific Bulb Society, Zephyranthes species wiki page

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in late spring once soil has warmed, in well-drained soil in full sun; lift or grow in containers where winters are colder than zone 8b.

directions: Habranthus ruber is a rare, first-described-in-1970 species from open fields and woodland edges in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, notable for flowers in a true scarlet-orange rather than the white-to-pink range typical of the genus. Flower spikes rise to about a foot tall in mid to late summer, each topped with one or two large blooms that open outfacing before drooping slightly on their second day. It is less cold-hardy than common Gulf Coast Habranthus such as H. robustus or H. tubispathus, so treat it as a collector's plant for zone 8b and warmer, or grow it in a pot that can be moved under cover in winter. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage and water during active summer growth, letting bulbs dry out through winter dormancy.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden blog, Habranthus ruber plant description
Pacific Bulb Society, Habranthus species wiki page

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in well-drained, sunny soil; mass plant for best display since individual flowers are thumb-sized.

directions: This South American variety of the widespread Habranthus tubispathus trades the species' usual copper-orange flowers for buds striped pink and rose on the outside that open to a pale pinkish-yellow, a distinctive color break within the copper lily complex. Narrow, insignificant grassy foliage gives little hint of the show to come until thumb-sized flowers emerge on short stems in midsummer. Because individual plants are small and the bulbs tiny, this variety reads best in a mass planting along a sunny rock garden edge or bed border rather than as a single specimen. Plant in full sun to light shade with sharp drainage and allow the clump to bulk up undisturbed for several seasons.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery, Habranthus tubispathus var. roseus plant description
